prompt: Halverd Freight requires every one of its employees to complete a one-day safety course before the end of the calendar year. The course is offered several times a month at each of the company's depots, and the personnel office issues a numbered certificate to each employee who completes it, without exception, on the day the course is completed. Marcus has worked at the Ashfield depot for the whole of this year, and the personnel office holds no certificate on file in his name. Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
options: The safety course is harder than most of Halverd's employees expect it to be.
Every employee who holds a numbered certificate has completed the safety course.
Marcus has not completed the safety course.
Nobody at the Ashfield depot told Marcus that the safety course was available.
Marcus will complete the safety course before the end of the calendar year.
explanation: Completing the course guarantees a certificate, so the absence of a certificate rules out completion. That is the contrapositive and the only conclusion the statements force. Reading the rule backward, so that a certificate proves completion, is a different claim, and nothing here rules out a certificate issued for some other reason. The difficulty of the course, what Marcus was told and what he will do next are matters the statements never touch.

prompt: The owner of the Bellamy Street cafe installed free wireless internet on the first of March, hoping to attract customers who would stay longer and order more while they worked. Sales for March came in twenty percent above the figure for February and above the figure for the same month a year earlier. In a note to her staff the owner wrote that the wireless internet was clearly responsible for the increase, and that she will therefore install it at the second branch she opens in the autumn. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the owner's reasoning?
options: Sales at two nearby cafes that offer no wireless internet fell slightly in March.
Several regular customers told the owner they were glad the internet was there.
The wireless installation cost considerably less than the owner had expected.
The cafe began opening two hours earlier on the first of March.
A number of the cafe's regular customers own neither a laptop nor a tablet.
explanation: A second change made on the same day gives the same rise a rival explanation, and two extra trading hours a day is easily large enough to account for a fifth more sales. Installation cost and customer goodwill leave the causal step untouched, and customers without a device were presumably buying coffee before March as well. A fall at cafes with no internet is the comparison the owner would want, so it supports her rather than weakening her.

prompt: The Vantry Community Library closes at seven o'clock each evening. In a survey distributed last term, sixty-two percent of the students enrolled at the nearby college said they would prefer a quiet place to study between seven and eleven at night, and a third of them said the space they use at home is too noisy for sustained work. The library board has proposed keeping the building open until eleven on weeknights. Because the extension answers a preference that students themselves reported, the board argues, the additional staffing cost is justified. Which of the following is an assumption on which the board's argument depends?
options: Enough students will come to the library during the added hours to justify what the extension costs.
The library has not tried extending its evening hours at any point in the past ten years.
No other building in Vantry or on the college campus stays open for study later than the library does at present.
Students who do their reading late at night retain more of it than students who do the same work in the morning.
Every student who answered the survey studies in the library at least once in a typical week.
explanation: A reported preference and an actual visit are not the same thing, and the board's case for the cost stands only if the stated demand turns into attendance. The library's past hours are history the argument does not rest on, and the reasoning needs no claim about rival study spaces in the town. Late reading producing better retention would be a bonus rather than a requirement, since the case rests on demand alone. The survey respondents need not already be regular library users for the extension to draw a crowd.

prompt: Kestlin Tools buys the steel blanks from which it presses its wrenches. In March the company replaced its longtime blank supplier with a new one that promised tighter thickness tolerances. Over the nine months that followed, the proportion of finished wrenches rejected by Kestlin's inspectors fell from six percent to four percent, the lowest figure the plant has recorded. Kestlin's operations manager has concluded that the change of supplier is what brought the rejection rate down, and she has recommended a three-year contract with the new supplier on that basis. Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the operations manager's conclusion?
options: Kestlin's rejection rate had been declining slowly but steadily for two years before the March change of supplier.
The new supplier's mill is close enough to Kestlin's plant that a delivery now takes one day rather than four.
The new supplier charges slightly more per blank than the previous supplier charged, and Kestlin has absorbed the difference.
The previous supplier had served Kestlin for more than a decade without a serious quality complaint.
Kestlin changed nothing else about its presses, its tooling or its inspection standards during those nine months.
explanation: The conclusion is causal, and its weakest point is that something else in the plant might explain the fall. Holding the presses, the tooling and the inspection standard constant across the same nine months removes the leading rivals and leaves the supplier as the change that remains. Delivery distance, price and the previous supplier's long record bear on whether the contract is a good deal rather than on what moved the rejection rate. A rate already falling for two years before the change would point at a trend, which cuts against the conclusion instead of supporting it.

prompt: The Harnwell Museum hangs its permanent collection in two rooms. When the north gallery was rearranged in the spring the curators applied a single condition to it, that every painting hung there be one produced after 1900, and the room has not been rehung since. The museum's oldest painting, which the catalog identifies by title and by date, hangs in the south gallery. The catalog records no dates for the other works in the south gallery. Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
options: The museum's oldest painting was produced at some point before 1900.
Every painting in the south gallery is older than every painting in the north.
The museum's oldest painting is not hanging in the north gallery.
The museum holds no painting at all that was produced before 1900.
The south gallery holds more paintings than the north gallery holds.
explanation: The statements place the oldest painting in the south gallery, so it is not in the north, and that is all they settle. The oldest painting could still date from 1950 if the whole collection is modern, so no date before 1900 follows, and for the same reason the museum may hold nothing at all from before 1900 or a great deal. The other works in the south gallery are undated in the catalog, so neither their ages nor their number can be compared with the north gallery's.

prompt:
Passage: "Urban planners have long debated whether adding road capacity relieves congestion. The phenomenon known as induced demand suggests it often does not. When a route becomes faster, journeys that were previously not worth making become worthwhile: a shopper who had ordered a delivery drives to the store instead, a commuter who had settled for a nearby employer accepts a better job further away, and drivers who had shifted to other routes or to earlier departure times come back to the widened road. Each of those is a trip the old road never carried. Within a few years traffic on the widened route frequently returns to something close to its former level, and the time savings that justified the work disappear.

The evidence most often cited comes from comparisons across metropolitan areas, where the total distance driven has risen almost in proportion to the lane miles built. Critics of that evidence point out that capacity is not added at random. Lanes go where growth is already expected, so some of the extra driving would have appeared with or without the construction. Researchers have tried to separate the two effects by studying capacity that was planned decades earlier, for reasons unconnected to present-day growth, and they continue to find a large response.

Some planners conclude from all this that road widening is futile, since the queue it was built to remove reassembles itself. Others accept every step of the account and draw the opposite lesson. The extra journeys, they argue, represent real economic activity that congestion had been suppressing, and the appropriate measure of success is the number of trips served rather than the speed at which any one of them is made. On that reading a road that fills up again has not failed. It has been used." According to the passage, what does induced demand describe?
options: Congestion returning to its earlier level a few years after a road is widened.
A permanent reduction in the total number of car journeys made.
Drivers choosing public transport when roads become congested.
New journeys appearing once a route becomes faster.
The tendency of construction costs to rise during a road project.
explanation: The passage defines it as journeys that were not worth making becoming worthwhile once the route speeds up, together with the return of drivers who had diverted. The other options describe effects the passage never attributes to induced demand. The return of traffic to its former level is the consequence the passage draws from induced demand, not the definition of the term itself.

prompt:
Passage: "Most songbirds are not born knowing their songs. A young male hears adult singing during a limited period early in life, stores what he hears, and then spends weeks practicing a rambling subsong that gradually converges on the model he memorized. Birds raised in isolation produce a crude and simplified song. Birds deafened after the memorizing period but before practice begins never converge on anything at all, which indicates that the young bird is matching his own output against a remembered target rather than unfolding a fixed motor program.

One consequence is that song varies by place. Neighboring populations of a single species often sing versions distinct enough that a trained listener can place a bird within a few valleys, and the boundaries between these dialects can be surprisingly sharp. Because each generation learns from the adults it happens to hear, a small variation introduced by one bird can spread through a local population and persist for decades after the bird that introduced it is gone.

Why the learning period closes is less settled. One account treats the closure as a fact about development: the circuits that support memorization mature, stabilize, and stop accepting new material, in much the way other sensory systems fix their wiring early and keep it. A second account treats the closure as an adaptation. A bird that kept revising its song would keep drifting away from the dialect its neighbors recognize, and a song that neighbors do not recognize is a poor advertisement to females and a poor warning to rivals. On the second view the window closes because a settled song is worth more than a flexible one, not because the machinery has worn out." According to the passage, what do birds deafened before practice begins demonstrate?
options: That a young bird compares the song it produces with a song it has stored.
That the period available for memorizing a song closes early in life.
That a bird raised in isolation sings a simpler song than other birds.
That neighboring populations of one species sing noticeably different songs.
That a variation introduced by one bird can persist for many decades.
explanation: A bird that cannot hear itself has the memorized model and nothing to compare against it, and the passage says such a bird never converges, so the comparison is what the practice period performs. The simplified song of an isolated bird shows that the model has to be heard, which is a separate point. Dialects, their persistence and the closing of the learning period are all discussed elsewhere in the passage and none of them rests on the deafening result.

prompt: Two years ago Hallum Freight introduced a three-day course in route planning and customer handling. Since then, drivers who completed the course have been promoted to the senior grade at nearly twice the rate of drivers who did not take it. Hallum's training director cites this gap as evidence that the course prepares drivers for the responsibilities of the senior grade, and she has asked the board to make the course a requirement for every driver the company employs. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the training director's argument?
options: The course is delivered online, and drivers work through it at home rather than at the depot where they report for duty.
Several drivers who completed the course described parts of the second day as repetitive.
The rate of promotion to the senior grade rose across every one of Hallum's departments during those same two years.
The course ran for three days rather than the five days its designers had originally proposed.
Depot managers nominate the drivers they consider strongest for the course, and nomination is required to attend.
explanation: The two groups were not formed by chance. If managers nominate the drivers they already rate highest, those drivers would have been promoted at a higher rate with no course at all, and the gap measures the nomination rather than the training. The delivery format, the shortened schedule and one repetitive day concern the quality of the course, not the comparison between the groups. A company wide rise in promotions lifts both groups together and so leaves the gap between them unexplained.

prompt: Between ten at night and five in the morning, the roads of Corran district carry about a tenth of the traffic they carry by day, yet they account for a quarter of the district's collisions. The district council has proposed installing lighting along the eleven kilometers of Corran road that are unlit at present, at a cost of roughly four million pesos. The council maintains that the lighting will bring the number of nighttime collisions down. Which of the following is an assumption on which the council's argument depends?
options: The collisions that occur on Corran's roads at night outnumber the collisions that occur on those same roads in daylight hours.
Drivers being unable to see clearly is part of what causes at least some nighttime collisions in the district.
Residents living along the unlit stretches of Corran road have asked the council more than once for better lighting.
Every nighttime collision in the district happens because a driver failed to see something on the road ahead.
Lighting is the least expensive of the road safety measures available to the council at the moment.
explanation: The proposal converts money into light, and light changes outcomes only if darkness is doing some of the damage. Should visibility play no part at all, the lighting would leave the collision count where it is. Whether night collisions outnumber daytime ones is a comparison the argument never uses, and cost ranking and local requests are reasons to act rather than links in the reasoning. Requiring poor visibility to explain every nighttime collision states far more than the conclusion needs.

prompt: Of the 200 households on Merrow Lane, 130 subscribe to the town's weekly newspaper and 90 keep a dog. Every household that keeps a dog and also subscribes to the paper received a free calendar from the paper in January. Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
options: Most of the households on Merrow Lane that keep a dog also subscribe to the weekly newspaper.
Exactly twenty households on Merrow Lane received a free calendar from the paper in January.
Every household on Merrow Lane either subscribes to the newspaper or keeps a dog, or does both.
The paper sent more free calendars to Merrow Lane in January than it sent to any other street.
At least twenty households on Merrow Lane both subscribe to the paper and keep a dog.
explanation: There are 200 households, and 130 plus 90 is 220, so at least 20 households have to be counted in both groups. That is the smallest overlap the numbers allow and the only conclusion the statements force. The overlap could be as large as 90, so the number of calendars is not fixed at twenty and dog owners need not mostly subscribe. Nor must every household fall into one group or the other, since an overlap of forty would leave twenty households in neither. A comparison with other streets rests on figures the statements never supply.

prompt: For one year the Aldworth branch of Tessen Insurance let its staff set their own start and finish times within a fixed daily total. At the end of the year, staff at Aldworth rated their satisfaction with the company at 7.8 out of ten, against a company average of 6.1. Tessen's head of operations has proposed extending the arrangement to all fourteen branches, on the ground that doing so will raise satisfaction across the company as a whole. Which of the following is an assumption on which the head of operations' proposal depends?
options: Satisfaction with the company is the measure that best predicts how long Tessen's staff stay with it.
Staff at Tessen's other thirteen branches have already asked to be allowed to set their own working hours.
Every member of the Aldworth staff preferred the flexible arrangement to the fixed hours it replaced.
Aldworth does not differ from the other branches in a way that would explain its higher satisfaction.
Flexible hours are no harder for a branch manager to administer than a fixed schedule is.
explanation: The proposal generalizes from one branch to fourteen, which holds only if Aldworth's result came from the hours rather than from something peculiar to Aldworth. Should the branch be younger, better managed or differently staffed, the gap may not travel. Unanimity at Aldworth and requests from the other branches would both be welcome and neither is required. What satisfaction predicts, and how hard the arrangement is to administer, bear on whether the change is worth making rather than on whether it will raise satisfaction.

prompt: Two years ago the city of Doverel began a recycling campaign, placing sorting bins on residential streets and mailing an illustrated guide to every household. Doverel measures its performance by the tonnage its trucks deliver to the regional landfill, and that figure fell by eleven percent last year, the first decline since the landfill opened. The city's environment office has reported the campaign a success and has asked the council to fund a second campaign of the same design in the neighboring district. Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the environment office's conclusion?
options: How much the city spent on designing and mailing the campaign's materials.
Whether the total quantity of waste Doverel generated also fell last year.
Which of Doverel's neighborhoods received the campaign materials earliest.
Whether most residents of Doverel say that they support recycling in principle.
How many residents remember seeing the campaign's advertisements last year.
explanation: Landfill tonnage falls when residents sort more and also when they throw less away in the first place, so the answer to this question either supports the office's reading or supplies the whole of the decline without it. Spending, rollout order and advertising recall measure the campaign's reach and cost rather than its effect on the tonnage. Support in principle is an attitude, and residents have held attitudes about recycling for years without the landfill figure moving.

prompt:
Passage: "For much of the twentieth century, economists treated the firm as a rational actor that minimizes costs. Behavioral research has complicated that picture. Studies of managerial decision-making find that executives often persist with failing projects, committing further resources in order to justify what has already been spent. This pattern, sometimes called escalation of commitment, is hard to reconcile with pure cost minimization, because money already spent cannot be recovered and should therefore carry no weight in a decision about what to do next.

The evidence is not confined to the laboratory. Analyses of capital budgeting inside large firms find that a project with an unfavorable interim review is approved for further funding more often when the reviewing manager is the same person who approved the original proposal. Auditors of failed technology programs describe an identical sequence: a deadline slips, more staff are assigned, the revised deadline slips again, and the program is then defended in terms of the sum it has already consumed.

Defenders of the traditional model respond that persistence may be rational in a different sense. Canceling a project publicly is a dated admission that an earlier judgment was wrong, and a manager whose next position depends on a record of completed work has reason to postpone that admission. On this reading the manager is optimizing after all, but the thing being optimized is a career rather than the firm's balance sheet. The behavior looks irrational only if the analyst assumes that the decision maker and the firm want the same thing.

The reply is not a full defense of the original model, since it concedes that the firm's costs are not what the manager is minimizing. What it does suggest is that the choice on offer is between two accounts of whose interests a decision serves, rather than between reason and error." What is the primary purpose of the passage?
options: To trace how the view economists take of the firm changed across the twentieth century.
To present a challenge to a traditional model and a response to that challenge.
To recommend specific practices that managers should adopt when projects fail.
To argue that the traditional economic model of the firm should be abandoned entirely.
To describe a series of experiments conducted on executives at large firms.
explanation: The passage lays out the traditional view, presents behavioral evidence against it, and then gives the traditional side's reply. It stops short of endorsing either position or recommending anything. Nor is the passage a chronology of the discipline: it sets out one challenge and one reply rather than a sequence of changing views.

prompt:
Passage: "For most of the twentieth century a factory held inventory the way a household holds a pantry. Parts arrived in large lots, sat in a warehouse, and were drawn down as the line needed them. The buffer absorbed everything: a late delivery, a bad batch, a machine that stopped. It also concealed the causes. A plant that can always reach for another bin has little reason to find out why the last bin was defective.

The alternative, developed in postwar Japanese manufacturing and adopted widely afterward, delivers parts in small quantities shortly before they are used. The immediate saving is the capital tied up in stock and the floor space it occupies. Supporters have generally argued that the larger gain is informational. With no buffer, a defect stops the line within hours instead of surfacing weeks later in a finished product, and the plant is forced to trace it to its source. Inventory, on this view, is not merely idle money. It is an anesthetic.

Critics of the system have concentrated on what happens when supply fails. A plant holding two days of parts cannot absorb a port closure, a fire at a supplier, or a shortage that lasts a quarter, and the firms that had driven their stock lowest were the ones that stopped first when several such disruptions arrived in succession.

Defenders reply that the criticism confuses the method with one way of applying it. Nothing in the approach requires a single supplier on another continent, and a firm may hold a deliberate buffer at each point where failure is both plausible and expensive while running the rest of the line lean. What the critics have identified, on this reading, is a purchasing decision that spread alongside the method rather than a defect in the method itself." In replying to the critics, the defenders of the method do which of the following?
options: Deny that firms holding little stock were harmed by the disruptions.
Separate the method itself from a purchasing practice that accompanied it.
Concede that the informational gain has been considerably overstated.
Argue that the capital saved outweighs the cost of a stopped line.
Claim that disruptions of the kind the critics describe are too rare to plan for.
explanation: The reply grants the harm and locates its cause elsewhere, in the choice of a distant single supplier, which the defenders say the method does not require. They therefore neither deny the harm nor call the disruptions rare. They also do not weigh saved capital against a stopped line, and far from conceding that the informational gain was overstated, they leave that claim standing and defend it.

prompt: A study of ninety mid-sized cities found that the cities in the top quarter for park area per resident scored, on average, nine points higher on a standard wellbeing index than the cities in the bottom quarter. The report's authors conclude that building parks raises the wellbeing of a city's residents, and they recommend that cities holding little parkland acquire vacant land and convert it. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the authors' conclusion?
options: Cities with higher tax revenue both build more parkland and score higher on wellbeing, for reasons unrelated to parks.
Some residents of the cities that have the most parkland per person visit a park only a few times in the course of a year.
The study measured park area rather than counting the number of separate parks in each city.
The wellbeing surveys were administered in different months in different cities, and index scores rise slightly in summer.
The budgets that the studied cities devote to maintaining their parks vary by a factor of four.
explanation: A correlation between two effects of a third thing is no evidence that either causes the other. If municipal wealth produces both the parkland and the wellbeing, the recommendation rests on nothing, because a poor city that converts vacant land acquires the park without acquiring the wealth. Measuring area rather than counting parks is the better of the two choices, not a defect. Infrequent visits, seasonal survey timing and uneven maintenance budgets add noise to the finding without touching the direction of the causal claim.

prompt: The Marine Institute has assembled a panel of six to review the coastal habitat survey submitted by a consulting firm. A commentator objects that the review should be set aside before it begins. Not one of the panel's members has published a paper in a marine biology journal, he notes, and the panel is therefore not competent to judge the survey's methods or its findings. The institute should, in his view, appoint a new panel before it accepts anything the current one reports. Which of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the commentator's reasoning?
options: It relies on a sample of published work far too small to support the general conclusion drawn from it.
It draws a conclusion about an entire group from evidence concerning a single member of that group.
It takes the order in which two events occurred as evidence that the earlier one caused the later one.
It treats publication in a field as the only way a person could become competent in it.
It uses a key term in one sense in its premise and in a different sense in its conclusion.
explanation: Competence can come from fieldwork, from laboratory practice, from training or from a neighboring discipline, and the commentator counts none of it. Treating an unpublished record as proof of incompetence is the step that does not hold. No sample is drawn, the evidence covers all six members rather than one, no causal claim about ordering is made, and no term shifts its meaning between the premise and the conclusion.

prompt: Verrow, an online retailer, replaced its checkout page in April. The new page asks for payment details on a single screen instead of three. In the month after the launch, the share of visitors who reached the checkout and went on to complete a purchase rose from 42 percent to 50 percent. Verrow's product team has concluded that the redesign is what produced the increase, and it has proposed rebuilding the account registration page along the same lines. Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the product team's conclusion?
options: Visitors randomly shown the old checkout page during that same month completed far fewer purchases.
Several specialists in interface design have praised the new checkout page in trade publications.
Completed purchases in the month before the launch stood at their usual level for that time of year.
Verrow's advertising spending and its mix of advertising channels were unchanged throughout the month.
The new checkout page loads about a fifth of a second faster than the page that it replaced.
explanation: A comparison group drawn at random within the same month holds constant everything else that changed in April, including the season, the advertising and the mix of visitors arriving at the site. That is a stronger warrant than closing rival explanations one at a time. Praise from specialists and a faster load are both consistent with the redesign doing nothing to completions. A normal seasonal baseline and unchanged advertising each remove one alternative, which helps, but neither reaches as far as a concurrent randomized comparison does.

prompt: A regional airline operates three routes out of Pellon. On every day last month the Pellon to Casterly flight carried more passengers than the Pellon to Ostrey flight, and the Pellon to Ostrey flight carried more passengers than the Pellon to Rill flight. Across the month the three routes together carried 24,000 passengers, and the airline canceled no flight on any route. Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
options: The Casterly route carried more than eight thousand passengers over the course of the month.
The Rill route carried fewer than six thousand passengers over the course of the month.
The Casterly route carried at least twice as many passengers last month as the Rill route did.
The Ostrey route carried exactly eight thousand passengers over the course of the month.
The Casterly flights were fuller, measured as a share of the seats on board, than the Rill flights.
explanation: The daily ordering carries over to the monthly totals, so the Casterly total is the largest of the three. If the largest of three numbers that sum to twenty four thousand were eight thousand or less, the three could not reach twenty four thousand at all, so the Casterly total must exceed that figure. The Rill total is bounded above but is not forced below six thousand, no route's total is pinned to any particular number, and nothing in the statements reports how many seats any aircraft carries.

prompt: The Veren valley grows about 1.4 million tons of grain, roots and vegetables in a year, while the food consumed by everyone living in the valley amounts to roughly 900,000 tons. A regional commissioner has drawn the conclusion that hunger in the valley is a problem the valley has already solved, and he has recommended that the province direct its food assistance to districts elsewhere. Which of the following is an assumption on which the commissioner's recommendation depends?
options: The valley's farms will produce at least as much in coming years as they produce now.
Every household in the valley can afford to buy as much food as the people in it require.
The valley brings in no food at all from the farming districts that surround it.
The valley's farms grow the same varieties of crop as the farms in the neighboring districts do.
The food the valley grows reaches the people within the valley who need to eat it.
explanation: Totals say nothing about who receives what, and a valley can grow a surplus while some of the people in it go without. The conclusion needs the food to reach those in need, whether by sale, by wage or by gift. Future output, imports from the surrounding districts and the varieties grown are not links the reasoning uses. Universal ability to pay would settle the matter but states more than the argument requires, since food can reach people without being bought.

prompt:
Passage: "Antibiotic resistance is often described as a crisis of the near future, but the mechanism behind it is old. Bacteria have carried and traded resistance genes for as long as antibiotics have existed in nature, which is far longer than they have existed in medicine. Soil frozen before the first clinical use of penicillin holds organisms with resistance genes, and so do bacteria recovered from caves and sediments that no manufactured drug has ever reached.

What has changed is the intensity of selection. A resistance gene is not free. It usually costs the cell something to carry, which is why resistant strains do not simply take over in the absence of a drug. Introduce the drug and the accounting reverses. Antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria efficiently, so the survivors inherit a population with their competition removed, and a gene that was rare becomes common within a few bacterial generations. Widespread clinical prescribing and routine agricultural use apply that pressure to enormous populations, continuously, in hospitals, in livestock, and in the water that leaves both.

Reducing total antibiotic use is therefore the primary lever available. It is also politically difficult. The benefit of restraint is diffuse and delayed. It is spread across every future patient and can never be credited to any particular decision not to prescribe. The cost falls immediately and visibly on the individual patient who is told that a prescription would do no good, or on the farmer asked to raise animals without a routine additive in the feed. Programs that succeed tend to be the ones that move the decision away from that encounter, by setting prescribing rules for a whole hospital or by regulating agricultural use directly, rather than by appealing to restraint one consultation at a time." According to the passage, what has changed in recent times?
options: The willingness of farmers to reduce their use of antibiotics.
Bacteria have only recently developed the ability to exchange genes.
The intensity of selection favoring resistant bacteria.
The efficiency with which antibiotics kill the bacteria that are susceptible to them.
The speed at which new antibiotics can be brought to market.
explanation: The passage says the mechanism is old and identifies intensity of selection as what has changed. It explicitly denies that gene exchange is new, and never discusses development speed or a change in willingness. Efficient killing of susceptible bacteria is how the selection works, not the thing the passage says has changed.

prompt:
Passage: "A painting that has hung for three centuries is not the object that left the studio. Varnish yellows, glazes abrade, earlier restorers have repainted losses in colors that have since shifted, and the wooden support has moved with every change of season. A conservator asked to clean such a picture is therefore not uncovering an original that waited intact beneath the grime. She is choosing, among several defensible states, the one the picture will now occupy.

The traditional case for thorough cleaning is that the artist's own surface is the only state with a claim to authority and that everything above it is accretion. Against this, an older European school held that centuries of settled varnish belong to the work as it has been received, and that stripping them substitutes a modern appetite for bright color in place of the muted harmony that generations actually saw. The argument has been fought most publicly over pictures whose cleaned state proved far more vivid than anyone had predicted.

Both positions share an assumption that recent decades have weakened, namely that one correct state exists and the conservator's task is to identify it. Analytical work has made the alternative harder to avoid. Cross sections show that some artists varnished their own pictures and toned those varnishes deliberately, so the line between the artist's surface and later accretion is not always a line at all, and in some pictures nobody can locate it.

The response has been procedural rather than doctrinal. An intervention is expected to be reversible where reversibility is possible, documented in full where it is not, and limited to what the present condition of the object requires. None of that settles which state is authentic. It shifts the burden onto the conservator to record what was done, so that a later judgment is not foreclosed by this one." The passage indicates that the procedural response described in the final paragraph does which of the following?
options: Establishes the artist's own surface as the state a cleaning should recover.
Shows that the boundary between original surface and accretion can be located.
Settles the dispute by showing that one of the two schools rests on an error.
Leaves a later conservator free to reach a judgment that differs from this one.
Forbids any intervention whose effects cannot afterward be undone.
explanation: The passage says outright that the procedure does not settle which state is authentic and that its point is to keep a later judgment from being foreclosed, which is what full documentation buys. It therefore does not decide for the artist's surface and does not resolve the dispute. It asks for reversibility only where reversibility is possible, so an irreversible step is documented rather than forbidden, and the analytical work is cited for the opposite of a locatable boundary.

prompt: Ostrel, a music streaming service, surveys its users each spring. Premium subscribers, who pay a monthly fee, rate the service at 8.4 out of ten, while users on the free tier rate it at 5.9. Ostrel's growth team has proposed offering free tier users a year of the premium service at a steep discount, reasoning that moving those users up will raise satisfaction across the whole user base and reduce the number of people who leave. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the growth team's reasoning?
options: The satisfaction survey is sent to premium subscribers twice a year and to free tier users once a year.
Premium subscribers listen for more hours in a typical week than free tier users listen in that week.
The users who upgrade are drawn from those already most satisfied with the free tier.
Premium subscribers pay a monthly fee that free tier users have so far chosen not to pay.
Some features of the premium tier are offered to free tier users during a two-week trial.
explanation: The gap may record who upgraded rather than what upgrading does. If the most satisfied users are the ones who move up, then satisfaction produced the upgrade, and pushing the rest up carries none of it with them. That the premium tier costs money is already implied by the setup. Sending the survey at different rates is a real bias but a small one, and a two-week trial would narrow the measured gap rather than create it. Heavier listening among premium subscribers is what one would expect if the upgrade did work, so it does not undercut the proposal.

prompt: The province is considering a levy of two pesos per liter on drinks with added sugar. In the three provinces that have imposed a similar levy, sales of the taxed drinks fell between fifteen and twenty percent within a year, and they have not recovered since. The health department argues that the levy will therefore bring down the rate of obesity among the province's adults over the coming decade. Which of the following is an assumption on which the health department's argument depends?
options: Consumers will not replace the drinks they give up with other products of similar calorie content.
The revenue the levy raises will be spent on programs that promote better diet and more physical activity.
The levy will apply to every drink with added sugar that is sold anywhere in the province.
Drinks with added sugar are the largest single source of calories in the average adult diet.
Producers will pass the whole of the levy through to shelf prices as soon as the measure takes effect.
explanation: The argument runs from a fall in sales to a fall in obesity, and that step holds only if the calories go away along with the drinks. Should buyers move to juice, to sweetened coffee or to snacks, the taxed drinks lose sales and waistlines stay where they were. The department does not need sugary drinks to be the largest source of calories, only a source worth reducing. Nor does it need the levy to reach every product without exception, or the revenue to be spent in any particular way, or the pass-through to be immediate.

prompt: Two years ago Merrow General Hospital adopted a surgical checklist requiring the team to confirm the patient's identity, the site of the operation and the count of instruments both before and after each procedure. An independent audit of operating room video found that errors of the kind the checklist targets fell by more than half in the year after it was introduced. Over that same year, however, the complication rate the hospital reports to the regional health authority rose from 3.1 percent to 4.4 percent. Which of the following, if true, best explains the discrepancy described above?
options: The hospital performed slightly fewer operations that year than the year before.
Several of the hospital's surgeons said the checklist made them more careful.
The checklist added several minutes to the preparation before each operation.
The checklist added a form on which complications formerly left unrecorded are logged.
Many of the hospital's surgeons were skeptical of the checklist when it was proposed.
explanation: A reported rate can climb while the underlying rate falls if the hospital has started counting cases it used to miss, which dissolves the discrepancy without disputing either figure. A slightly smaller number of operations changes the denominator of both measures together and so explains neither. Longer preparation and early skepticism concern how the checklist was received. Surgeons reporting greater care fits the fall in errors and leaves the rise in reported complications exactly as puzzling as before.

prompt: At last week's board meeting the chief executive of Landry Instruments made the case for a cut. Orders have fallen for three consecutive quarters, she said, and the company holds enough cash for eleven months of operation at its present rate of spending. Research consumes a third of that spending. Either the board cuts the research budget by a third, she argued, or Landry will run short of cash before demand recovers. No director on this board is willing to see the company fail. The board must therefore approve the cut when it votes this month. Which of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the chief executive's reasoning?
options: It uses a key term in one sense in its premise and in another in its conclusion.
It treats two courses of action as the only ones open to the company.
It mistakes a condition that is necessary for one that is by itself sufficient.
It generalizes from a sample unlikely to represent the population drawn from.
It rests on the judgment of a person who is not an expert on the matter at issue.
explanation: A choice between two options binds only when there is no third, and the chief executive closes off none of the obvious alternatives. A company in a downturn can raise capital, defer other spending, sell a product line, slow its hiring or cut research by less than a third. No term shifts meaning between the premise and the conclusion, no sample is drawn, and nothing is treated as sufficient that is merely necessary. Her own standing is not in question either, since the objection is to the structure of the choice she offers.

prompt: Corran Analytics filled a number of positions this spring. Under the firm's hiring policy an applicant had to pass a written test before being scheduled for an interview, and the policy was applied without exception, so every applicant who was interviewed had passed the test. One of the specialties the test covered turned out to have no vacancy at all this year, and some applicants who passed the written test were not offered a position. Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
options: Some applicants who were interviewed were not offered a position.
Some applicants were not offered a position.
Every applicant who passed the written test was interviewed at some stage.
No applicant was offered a position without first being interviewed.
Some applicants who passed the written test were interviewed.
explanation: One premise states outright that some applicants passed the test and were not offered a position, so some applicants were not offered a position. Nothing else here is guaranteed. Interviewees are a subset of those who passed, not the reverse, so the passers need not all have been interviewed, and the rejected passers could be exactly the people who never reached an interview. The policy makes a pass a condition of an interview and says nothing about what an offer requires. It is not even guaranteed that anyone was interviewed.

prompt: Counts of breeding songbirds in the Aldern basin have fallen by about half since 1975. Application of the insecticides now in widest agricultural use began in the basin in the early 1970s and reached its present level by 1980. An ornithologist has argued that the insecticides are the cause of the decline, pointing to the overlap between the two periods and to laboratory work showing that the compounds are toxic to small birds. Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the ornithologist's argument?
options: Application of the same insecticides in the basin rose again in the 1990s, after the decline was well under way.
The firms that manufacture the insecticides expanded their production capacity sharply during the 1970s.
Songbird numbers have held steady in a similar neighboring basin where the insecticides were never used.
Several other bird species in the basin have also declined somewhat over the same period.
Farmers in the basin report larger harvests in the years since they began applying the insecticides.
explanation: Coincident timing is weak evidence on its own, because a great deal else changed in the basin over those years. A comparable basin that lacks the insecticide and lacks the decline supplies the missing comparison and is the nearest thing to a control that field evidence allows. Production capacity and harvest size concern the insecticides but say nothing about birds. Other species declining is consistent with the insecticide and with several other causes. A rise in application after the decline had begun runs against the timing the argument leans on.

prompt:
Passage: "The standard account of the industrial revolution credits technological invention. A sequence of machines appeared, and industry followed. Recent economic history has emphasized something less visible, namely the price of the things a machine replaces. In regions where wages were high relative to the price of fuel, a machine that burned coal in order to save labor paid for itself quickly. Where labor was cheap and fuel was dear, the same machine was a poor investment, and it was not bought.

The evidence assembled for this view is comparative. Wage series and fuel prices reconstructed for several eighteenth-century economies show a wide spread, with some regions paying skilled workers several times what their counterparts earned elsewhere while sitting on coalfields that made fuel unusually cheap. Early spinning and pumping machinery, on this reading, was installed first in exactly those places, and installed elsewhere only later, as improvements in design cut the fuel each machine consumed and made it profitable at lower wages. The invention was available in both settings. The reason to use it was not.

On this account the machines were not so much the cause of industrial change as the response to it, and the question worth asking shifts from why the inventions were made to why they were worth installing.

Critics of the wage explanation raise two objections. The first is empirical. There are documented cases of adoption running ahead of any wage advantage that can be shown, which the account ought not to permit. The second objection is that the explanation understates why the inventions existed to be adopted at all. Scientific societies, instrument makers and a culture of published experiment made a whole class of machines thinkable, and no arrangement of prices will produce a machine that nobody has yet designed." Which of the following best expresses the wage explanation described in the passage?
options: High wages relative to fuel costs made mechanization commercially worthwhile.
Machines were invented in regions where scientific institutions were strongest.
Mechanization spread fastest in the regions where fuel was expensive relative to wages.
Workers in high-wage regions actively resisted the introduction of machinery.
Technological invention was the primary driver of industrial change.
explanation: The passage states that where wages were high relative to fuel prices, replacing labor with machines paid for itself, which is the wage explanation in a sentence. The institutions option belongs to the critics, and the invention-first option is the standard account the passage is contrasting with. The option that reverses the ratio, setting expensive fuel against cheap labor, inverts the condition the passage actually states.

prompt:
Passage: "Scores on standardized intelligence tests rose steadily through most of the twentieth century in every country whose records run long enough to measure the change. The rise was large, roughly three points a decade on the usual scale, and it fell mainly on the parts of the test that ask for abstract classification and pattern completion rather than on vocabulary or arithmetic. Because publishers renormalize their scales every few decades, the increase was invisible to anyone comparing scores within a single edition, and it came to light only when old and new versions were given to the same people.

The finding is awkward for any account that treats a test score as a fixed measure of an underlying capacity. Taken at face value it implies that the average person of a century ago would score near the threshold once used to identify serious impairment, which the historical record of that period plainly does not support.

The leading explanation holds that what rose is not general capacity but familiarity with one particular way of handling a question. Schooling, clerical work and a scientific vocabulary all train people to treat a problem as an abstraction to be sorted by rule, rather than as a concrete situation to be described from experience, and the subtests that gained most are exactly the ones that reward that habit. On this account the tests measure something real and worth measuring, but something narrower and more historically contingent than the word intelligence suggests.

The account carries a prediction that can be checked. If the gains come from the spread of abstract habits of mind through schooling and office work, they should slow or halt in populations where that spread has already run its course, and several countries with long educational records have reported flat or falling scores since the 1990s." Which of the following findings would most undermine the leading explanation described in the passage?
options: Gains of similar size in populations whose schooling and work changed little.
Publishers renormalized their scales more often than the passage reports.
Average scores in several long-schooled countries have stopped rising.
People of a century ago would score poorly on a test written today.
Gains were larger on abstract classification than on vocabulary subtests.
explanation: The explanation makes the gains a byproduct of schooling and office work, so an equal gain where neither changed leaves the proposed cause with nothing to do. The uneven pattern across subtests and the recent flattening are both offered in the passage as support for the explanation rather than against it. Poor scores for people of a century ago restate the puzzle the explanation was built to answer, and how often a scale is renormalized bears on when the rise was noticed, not on what caused it.

prompt: Last year the publisher Vantry and Hale commissioned a new cover style for its paperback list and applied that style to eighteen of the sixty titles it reissued during the year. Across the fourth quarter those eighteen titles sold on average forty percent more copies than the reissued titles that kept the previous style. The publisher's marketing director has concluded that the new covers caused the difference, and she has proposed extending the style to the whole list before the spring catalog goes to print. Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the marketing director's conclusion?
options: Which printing house produced the covers for the eighteen reissued titles.
How much the publisher paid the designer who developed the new cover style.
Whether the new covers use colors that stand out on a crowded shelf.
Whether the eighteen titles were already expected to outsell the other reissues.
Whether readers say they notice cover designs while browsing in a shop.
explanation: The eighteen titles were selected rather than drawn at random, so the gap measures the covers only if the two groups were comparable to begin with. An answer either removes that rival explanation or supplies it whole. The designer's fee and the printing house have no bearing on why those titles sold. Standing out on a shelf and what readers say they notice speak to the merits of the design in general rather than to why these particular titles outsold the rest.

prompt:
Passage: "Tardigrades, the microscopic animals sometimes called water bears, survive conditions that kill almost everything else. Dried to less than one percent of their normal water content, they enter a state called cryptobiosis in which no measurable metabolism occurs. In that state they have endured temperatures near absolute zero, pressures greater than those at the bottom of the deepest ocean trench, and doses of radiation hundreds of times what a person can tolerate. For decades the explanation offered was trehalose, a sugar that replaces water in cell membranes and holds their structure in place as the animal dries. Trehalose does exactly that in brine shrimp and in some yeasts, and the analogy was inviting.

The trouble is that many tardigrade species produce almost no trehalose at all. Researchers looking for what else might be responsible identified a family of proteins found in no other animal. Unlike ordinary proteins, these have no fixed shape while the cell is wet. As water leaves, they vitrify: the cytoplasm becomes a glass rather than a liquid, immobilizing the molecules suspended in it and preventing the collisions that would otherwise tear them apart. Silencing the genes for these proteins leaves the animals unable to survive drying, and inserting the same genes into yeast makes yeast substantially more tolerant of desiccation.

Whether this fully explains tardigrade resilience remains unsettled. Vitrification accounts for survival of drying, but not obviously for survival of radiation, which damages DNA directly and does not depend on water loss. Some laboratories have proposed a separate protein that binds to DNA and shields it. Others suspect that the two capacities are linked, since much radiation damage is done indirectly by reactive molecules that a glassy interior would immobilize along with everything else." According to the passage, what happens inside a tardigrade cell as the animal dries?
options: The cytoplasm becomes a glass that holds the molecules suspended in it in place.
Trehalose accumulates in the membranes and takes the place of the water that is leaving the cell.
Reactive molecules are expelled from the cell before they can reach and damage the animal's DNA.
The animal's unusual proteins are broken down and their components are recycled into new membranes.
The internal temperature falls until it approaches absolute zero and metabolism stops.
explanation: The passage states that the unusual proteins vitrify as water leaves, so the cytoplasm becomes a glass rather than a liquid and the suspended molecules are immobilized. Trehalose is named as the old explanation that fails because many species produce almost none of it. Expelling reactive molecules, recycling proteins, and a fall in temperature are never described as things the cell does.

prompt:
Passage: "Before standardized containers, loading a cargo ship was a craft. Dockworkers stacked barrels, sacks, crates and drums by hand, fitting irregular shapes together in a hold the way stones are fitted into a wall. A ship might spend more days at a dock than at sea, and the cost of moving goods was dominated not by the ocean voyage but by the two ends of it. Estimates from the period put port handling at roughly half the total cost of an international shipment.

The container changed that arithmetic, but not because the box itself was clever. A steel box is a simple object, and versions of it had run on railways for decades. What mattered was agreement. A container is useful only if the crane at the far port can lift it, the truck chassis can carry it, and the ship's cell guides can hold it, which means the corner fittings, the dimensions and the lifting points must be identical everywhere. Reaching that agreement took nearly twenty years of negotiation among carriers, railroads, unions and national standards bodies, several of which had already invested in incompatible designs and preferred their own.

The consequences reached well beyond the docks. Once distance became cheap, a factory no longer had to sit near its customers or its suppliers, and production could be broken into stages performed in different countries. Historians of the period tend to argue that the container did not merely lower a cost but rearranged where things are made. The ports moved too, since the old finger piers built for hand loading could not accommodate the cranes and the acres of stacking yard that the new system required." The passage is primarily concerned with:
options: explaining the engineering difficulties that had to be solved before a steel cargo box could be built.
arguing that the container mattered because of the standards agreed for it rather than the box itself.
describing how the decline of the old finger piers reshaped the economies of port cities everywhere.
comparing the cost of moving goods by ocean with the cost of moving the same goods by rail.
criticizing the carriers, railroads and unions whose incompatible designs delayed a needed reform.
explanation: The second paragraph says outright that the box is a simple object and that what mattered was agreement on identical fittings, dimensions and lifting points, and the rest of the passage traces the consequences of that agreement. Engineering difficulty is explicitly denied, and the piers, the rail comparison and the delay are details in service of that point rather than the point itself.

prompt:
Passage: "Economists trying to measure how much unpaid work households perform have relied for decades on the time-use diary, in which a respondent records what he or she was doing during each interval of a single day. The instrument is simple and its three well known weaknesses are easy to state. People forget short tasks, they round durations to convenient numbers, and they are reluctant to record activities they consider idle or embarrassing.

Two of these problems have been reduced by technology. Prompts delivered to a telephone at random intervals catch short tasks that a diary written up at the end of the day misses, and automatic time stamps remove the rounding. The third has proved more stubborn. Respondents remain unwilling to record certain activities, and the bias is not uniform: studies comparing diaries against direct observation find that the gap is widest for activities carrying some social judgment, and that it differs by gender in ways that vary from country to country.

This matters because time-use diaries are the main source for national estimates of the value of household production, a figure that some governments now publish alongside conventional output measures. If the underreporting is uneven, the resulting estimates are not merely imprecise but systematically tilted, and comparisons between countries may reflect differences in what people are willing to write down rather than differences in what they do. Some statisticians therefore argue that observational studies, though far more expensive, should be run periodically to calibrate the diaries. Others reply that observation changes behavior in its own way, and that a bias which is at least stable over time is preferable to one that is unknown." According to the passage, which weakness of time-use diaries has NOT been substantially reduced by technology?
options: The tendency of respondents to round the durations they report to convenient numbers.
The failure of respondents to remember and record tasks of very short duration.
The reluctance of respondents to record activities that carry some social judgment.
The expense of running direct observational studies alongside the diaries themselves.
The difficulty of converting the entries in a diary into a monetary value.
explanation: The passage lists three weaknesses, says technology has reduced two of them, and identifies the third, unwillingness to record certain activities, as the stubborn one, adding that the gap is widest where social judgment attaches. Rounding and forgotten short tasks are the two named as reduced. Expense and monetary conversion are raised later and are not on the list of three.

prompt:
Passage: "Negligence law asks whether a defendant behaved as a reasonable person would have behaved in the circumstances. The standard is deliberately objective: it does not ask what this particular defendant believed was sensible, and a defendant who tried his best is liable anyway if his best fell short. Courts defend the objectivity on two grounds. It gives everyone a single, knowable rule, and it spares juries the impossible task of reconstructing an individual's mental world.

The objectivity is not absolute. A child is judged against other children of similar age and experience, and a defendant with a physical disability is judged against a reasonable person with that disability. A doctor is held to the standard of a competent doctor, not of a competent layperson. Critics observe that once these adjustments are admitted, the standard is doing something more complicated than it advertises: it is objective with respect to some characteristics of the defendant and subjective with respect to others, and the line between the two categories is drawn by courts rather than derived from any principle.

Defenders answer that the line is not arbitrary even if it is not derived. The characteristics that earn an adjustment are those the defendant could not have altered and could not reasonably have been expected to compensate for, while the characteristics that earn none, such as inexperience, carelessness or a hot temper, are precisely those the law wishes to give people a reason to work on. On this reading the standard is not a description of ordinary behavior at all. It is an instruction about the conduct the community will insist on, and the apparent inconsistency is the shape of a policy rather than the flaw of a definition." The reference to a doctor in the second paragraph serves primarily to:
options: argue that standards for professionals ought to be set by professional bodies rather than by courts.
show that different courts have applied the reasonable person standard inconsistently to similar facts.
suggest that defendants with expert training are treated more leniently than ordinary defendants are.
give a further instance of the standard being adjusted to a characteristic of the defendant.
illustrate how hard juries find it to reconstruct what was in a defendant's mind at the time.
explanation: The doctor sits in a short list with the child and the defendant with a physical disability, all offered as cases where the supposedly objective standard bends to something about the person being judged, which sets up the criticism that follows. Nothing in the passage says expert defendants are treated leniently, and the jury point belongs to the first paragraph as a defense of objectivity rather than an exception to it.

prompt:
Passage: "Software licenses that permit copying come in two broad families. Permissive licenses let anyone use the code for any purpose, including inside a product whose own source is never released. Reciprocal licenses, often called copyleft, attach a condition: anyone who distributes a modified version must release the modifications under the same terms. Both families rely on copyright rather than opposing it. A copyleft license is enforceable only because the author holds the exclusive right to control copying and has chosen to license that right conditionally.

The practical difference shows up in how companies behave. A firm that builds a product on permissive code may keep its own changes private, and many firms do, so improvements made inside the firm never return to the project. A firm that builds on copyleft code must publish its modifications if it ships the result, so the project receives the improvements, but some firms decline to build on that code at all. Neither outcome is obviously better for a project, and the two families have persisted side by side for thirty years without either displacing the other.

A complication has grown with the shift to software delivered over a network. Copyleft conditions are typically triggered by distribution, and a company that runs modified code on its own servers and offers the result as a service distributes nothing to anyone. The modifications stay private and the reciprocity the license was written to secure does not operate. Newer licenses attempt to close this by treating network access as a triggering event, but they are less widely adopted, partly because the obligation they create is harder for a company's lawyers to bound: it can reach code that was never intended to be shipped to anyone." It can be inferred from the passage that a company running modified copyleft software only on its own servers is:
options: in violation of its license for as long as it declines to publish the modifications it has made.
obliged to obtain a second, permissive license from the author before it may run the code at all.
barred by the terms of the original license from making any modifications to the code.
prevented by copyright law from offering the modified software to the public as a service.
not required by a distribution-triggered license to release its modifications.
explanation: The passage says the condition is triggered by distribution, that such a company distributes nothing, and that the modifications therefore stay private, which is why newer licenses had to invent a network trigger. That is the opposite of a violation, and nothing in the passage requires a second license, forbids modification, or bars offering the result as a service.

prompt:
Passage: "Adding soluble iron to certain regions of the open ocean triggers a bloom of phytoplankton within days. The chemistry behind this is settled. Large stretches of the Southern Ocean hold plenty of nitrate and phosphate but almost no iron, so iron is the limiting nutrient and a small addition produces a large biological response. Thirteen open-ocean experiments carried out between 1993 and 2009 confirmed the bloom in every case.

The proposal that follows is to use this response to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Phytoplankton take up carbon as they grow, and if enough of the resulting organic matter sinks below the depth at which water mixes back to the surface, that carbon is out of the atmosphere for centuries. The step that matters is therefore not the bloom but the sinking, and the sinking is exactly what the experiments measured least well. Most of the carbon fixed in a bloom is eaten by grazers or respired by bacteria within the upper hundred meters and returns to the surface within a year. Estimates of the fraction that reaches depth vary by more than a factor of ten between studies, and the studies with the most careful measurement generally report the lowest figures.

It is worth being precise about what this uncertainty licenses. It does not show that fertilization cannot sequester carbon, and the persistent claim that the experiments failed misrepresents them. What it shows is that the quantity a purchaser of carbon credits would be paying for has not been measured to anything approaching the accuracy such a market would require. Enthusiasm has run consistently ahead of the measurement, and the appropriate response is better measurement rather than either commercial deployment or dismissal." The author's attitude toward ocean iron fertilization is best described as:
options: unconvinced that the effect has been measured well enough to sell, yet unwilling to dismiss it.
confident that the method will prove to be an effective and cheap means of removing carbon.
persuaded by the thirteen experiments that the approach has been shown to be unworkable.
indifferent to the question, on the ground that the underlying chemistry is already settled.
critical of the scientists who designed and carried out the thirteen open-ocean experiments.
explanation: The closing paragraph refuses both endings: it says the uncertainty does not show that fertilization cannot work and that calling the experiments failures misrepresents them, while also saying the quantity a buyer would pay for is nowhere near well enough measured for a market. That is doubt about the measurement rather than confidence, dismissal, indifference or blame directed at the researchers.

prompt:
Passage: "Franchising solved a problem that troubled early chain retailers: how to grow quickly without either raising enormous capital or trusting distant salaried managers to work hard when nobody was watching. A franchisee buys the right to operate under the brand, supplies the capital for the outlet, and keeps the residual profit. Because the operator's own money is at stake, the monitoring problem largely dissolves. The franchisor collects a royalty on sales and spends its effort on the brand rather than on supervision.

The arrangement creates a second problem in place of the first. Each outlet's profit depends on its own service and cleanliness, but the value of the brand depends on all of them together. An operator who lets standards slip captures the whole saving and bears only a small share of the damage, which is spread across every other outlet in the system. Franchise contracts are therefore unusually detailed and unusually one-sided, specifying suppliers, hours, recipes and signs, and reserving broad rights of inspection and termination. Courts have generally enforced them, reasoning that the restrictions protect the asset the franchisee bought access to.

Economists have noted a pattern that follows from this logic. Franchising is most common where customers are travelers rather than residents, since a customer who will never return has no way to punish a bad outlet except by avoiding the brand everywhere. It is least common where the service is complex enough that quality cannot be specified in a contract. Where a location is both heavily traveled and highly visible, the franchisor tends to own the outlet outright, keeping under direct control those outlets whose failure would do the most damage to the brand." Based on the passage, which business would be LEAST likely to be organized as a franchise?
options: A chain of budget motels placed at intervals along a busy interstate highway.
A law practice whose attorneys handle unusual and complicated commercial disputes.
A chain of coffee shops operating inside the terminals of large regional airports.
A chain of quick-service restaurants located at rest stops on major highways.
A chain of car rental counters located in the concourses of busy railway stations.
explanation: The passage gives two conditions: franchising thrives where customers are travelers, and it is least common where the service is too complex to specify in a contract. Motels, airport coffee shops, highway restaurants and station rental counters all serve travelers with services that a detailed contract can describe. Unusual and complicated disputes are the case the passage explicitly puts outside the reach of a contract.

prompt:
Passage: "When speakers of mutually unintelligible languages are thrown together and need to trade, they improvise a pidgin: a stripped vocabulary borrowed mostly from the dominant group, almost no inflection, and word order that varies from one speaker to the next. A pidgin is nobody's first language. What interests linguists is what happens in the next generation. Children raised in a pidgin-speaking community do not learn a pidgin. They produce a creole, which has consistent word order, a system of markers for tense and aspect, embedded clauses, and the other machinery that pidgins lack.

One influential account treats this as evidence for an innate language faculty. On this view the children are not learning the grammar, because the grammar is not present in what they hear. They are supplying it, and the striking resemblances among creoles that arose on different continents from unrelated source languages reflect the shape of the faculty itself rather than any shared history.

The competing account does not deny that children build the grammar, only that they build it out of nothing. It points out that the adults around them were not speaking a uniform pidgin. Each spoke a pidgin shaped by his own first language, so the input was variable rather than empty, and a learner facing variable input has good reason to settle on whichever pattern is most frequent and most reliably understood. Similar solutions on different continents would then reflect similar pressures rather than a shared innate template.

Deciding between the accounts has been difficult because the historical record is thin. The pidgin stage is rarely documented, and it is precisely the input to the first creole-speaking generation that would have to be reconstructed. Studies of newly formed sign languages have been offered as a living substitute, though whether a deaf community's situation is comparable remains contested." The passage suggests that the two accounts disagree principally about:
options: whether a creole ends up with more grammatical structure than the pidgin that preceded it.
whether the children of a pidgin-speaking community acquire the pidgin as a first language.
the character of the linguistic input available to the first generation of creole speakers.
whether creoles that arose on different continents in fact resemble one another closely.
whether the newly formed sign languages now under study should be classified as creoles.
explanation: The second account is described as agreeing that children build the grammar and disputing only that they build it out of nothing, on the ground that the adult input was variable rather than empty. Both accounts accept that creoles are more structured than pidgins, that children do not acquire a pidgin as a first language, and that distant creoles resemble one another; the sign language question is raised as a possible way to settle the disagreement, not as its subject.

prompt:
Passage: "A patent claim is a sentence that marks a boundary. Anything inside it infringes, and anything outside it does not. The virtue of insisting on the literal words is notice: a competitor can read the claim and design around it with confidence. The vice is that an infringer who makes an insubstantial change escapes, and that a claim drafted years before a technology matured may not reach a variation nobody had thought to describe.

Most patent systems answer with a doctrine of equivalents, under which a device outside the literal words may still infringe if it performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. The doctrine is old and uneasy. Every application of it enlarges a boundary the public was invited to rely on, and the enlargement is discovered only after a court has ruled.

Courts have accordingly hedged the doctrine with limits. The most consequential is prosecution history estoppel. If, during examination, an applicant narrowed a claim in order to win allowance over the prior art, he may not later recapture the surrendered territory by calling the surrendered variation an equivalent. The rule is severe, and it is meant to be. The applicant chose the words, the public read the file, and the narrowing was the price of the grant.

The result is a system that is neither purely literal nor purely purposive, and commentators disagree about whether the balance is stable. Some argue that the estoppel rule has made the doctrine so hard to invoke that it no longer performs the function it was created to perform. Others reply that its value lies less in the cases it wins than in the cases it deters, which by their nature cannot be counted." The statement that the applicant chose the words and the public read the file serves primarily to:
options: criticize applicants who draft their claims carelessly during the examination process.
explain why patent claims are so often drafted years before a technology has matured.
question whether a doctrine of equivalents ought to be recognized by courts at all.
justify the severity of a rule the passage has just described as severe.
identify the disagreement among commentators about whether the present balance is stable.
explanation: The sentence comes immediately after the passage calls prosecution history estoppel severe and says the severity is intended, and it supplies the reasons for that intention: the applicant wrote the narrowing and the public relied on it.
