It is not an attack on careless drafting, not an argument against the doctrine of equivalents, and not the commentators' disagreement, which arrives in the following paragraph.

prompt:
Passage: "Measuring the distance to a remote galaxy requires an object whose true brightness is known, since apparent brightness then gives distance directly. A particular class of exploding star has served this purpose for three decades. These explosions occur when a dense stellar remnant draws matter from a companion until it passes a threshold mass and detonates, and because that threshold is set by physics rather than by circumstance, the explosions were expected to be nearly identical.

They are not identical, but they are correctable. Brighter examples fade more slowly, and a single empirical relation between peak brightness and rate of fading reduces the scatter enough to make these objects the most precise distance indicators available at large separations. It was this correction, applied to distant explosions in the late 1990s, that produced the evidence that the expansion of the universe is accelerating.

The correction is where the difficulty now sits. The relation between brightness and fade rate is empirical, calibrated on nearby explosions whose distances are known by other means, and then applied to distant ones that occurred in younger galaxies of different chemical composition. If the relation drifts with the age or composition of the host galaxy, the calibration carries an error along with the measurement, and that error would be systematic rather than random, so no amount of additional data would average it away. Surveys have looked for such a drift and have set limits on it, but the limits are not tight enough to be ignored in the current generation of measurements, where the disagreement between different methods of measuring the expansion rate now exceeds the quoted uncertainty of either.

Nothing here suggests the acceleration is an artifact. It suggests that the next advance will come from understanding the explosions rather than from observing more of them." The passage indicates that a drift in the brightness-fade relation would be especially troubling because it would:
options: leave the explosions too faint to be observed at the largest separations now under study.
establish that the expansion of the universe is not in fact accelerating after all.
force astronomers to give up empirical calibration in favor of purely theoretical models.
remove the present disagreement between different methods of measuring the expansion rate.
introduce an error that collecting more observations would not reduce.
explanation: The passage says the error would be systematic rather than random, so no amount of additional data would average it away, which is exactly why a drift is worse than ordinary imprecision. The passage explicitly denies that any of this shows the acceleration to be an artifact, and it neither predicts an abandonment of empirical calibration nor suggests that a drift would resolve the disagreement between methods.

prompt:
Passage: "Radio spectrum was for most of the twentieth century assigned by administrative hearing. An applicant argued that granting it a license would serve the public interest, and a regulator chose among the arguments. The procedure was slow, the criteria were vague, and the licenses that emerged were worth a great deal more than the applicants had paid for them, which is a description of a process that rewards advocacy rather than use.

Auctions replaced hearings in many countries during the 1990s, and the design problem turned out to be harder than it looked. Spectrum licenses are not independent goods. A carrier that wins a block covering one city and not the city next to it may have bought something close to worthless, so bidders need to express what they will pay for combinations rather than for single items. Selling each license separately by sealed bid forces every bidder to guess what the others will do and to risk winning half of what it needs, an exposure that makes cautious bidders bid low and aggressive ones overpay.

The response was the simultaneous ascending auction, in which every license stays open while bidding continues, so a bidder losing one piece of a plan can withdraw from the rest before the sale closes. It works, in the sense that it usually assigns licenses to the bidders that value them most and raises substantial revenue, but it introduced problems of its own. A long open auction lets bidders signal to one another through the trailing digits of their bids, and several regulators have had to write rules against the practice.

The literature that grew out of these sales is now cited well beyond spectrum. Its central lesson is that a market does not simply exist to be used. Its rules determine what it can express, and those rules have to be designed for the goods actually being sold." Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The rules of an auction, rather than the decision to hold one, determine how well spectrum is assigned.
Administrative hearings distributed radio spectrum more fairly than the auctions that replaced them.
The simultaneous ascending auction has eliminated the possibility of collusion among bidders.
Spectrum licenses ought to be sold one at a time rather than in combinations of several blocks.
Regulators in the 1990s badly underestimated the revenue that a spectrum sale could raise.
explanation: The passage moves from a bad assignment procedure to auctions, then spends most of its length on why the particular auction design mattered and how one design fixed an exposure problem while creating a signaling problem, closing with the statement that a market's rules determine what it can express. It never prefers hearings, never claims collusion was eliminated, and its argument about combinations runs against selling licenses one at a time.

prompt:
Passage: "For twenty years microcredit was described as a way out of poverty. Small loans, made mostly to women, without collateral and at interest rates far below those charged by local moneylenders, would fund small enterprises whose profits would raise household income. The claim rested largely on comparisons between borrowers and non-borrowers, which is a weak design: people who seek a loan differ from people who do not in ambition, in existing business activity and in access to information, and every one of those differences also predicts income.

A series of randomized evaluations conducted in six countries addressed that objection by randomizing which neighborhoods a lender entered. The results were consistent and modest. Borrowing rose, business investment rose somewhat, and household income and consumption were essentially unchanged. Measures of empowerment and of children's schooling moved very little. The pattern held across quite different settings, which is unusual enough to be worth noting on its own.

Two readings of the same result compete. The first is that microcredit does not do what was claimed for it, and that the enthusiasm reflected a narrative rather than evidence. The second is that the evaluations measured the wrong quantity. An average conceals a distribution, and a program that helps a minority substantially while leaving the majority unaffected produces exactly the average that was observed. Later analyses looking for such heterogeneity have found some, concentrated among households that already ran a business before the loan arrived.

What is no longer seriously disputed is the scale of the original claim. Microcredit is a useful financial instrument that lets a household manage timing, absorb a shock and avoid a moneylender, and that is not a small thing. It is not a mechanism for lifting large numbers of people out of poverty, and the evidence that it is has not appeared." The passage suggests that a lender seeking the largest income gains from microcredit should concentrate on:
options: neighborhoods that no lender of any kind has previously entered.
borrowers who have had no prior experience with any form of formal credit.
households that were already running a business before they borrowed.
households whose children are not at present enrolled in a school.
communities in which the local moneylenders charge the highest rates.
explanation: The third paragraph reports that later analyses did find gains concentrated in one group, and names it: households that already ran a business before the loan. The randomization was by neighborhood entry rather than by prior lending, and nothing in the passage links larger income gains to inexperience with credit, to school enrollment or to the rates charged by moneylenders.

prompt: The Riverton municipal library plans to convert its basement periodicals room into a study hall with forty desks. The periodicals will be moved to compact shelving on the second floor, which will require removing six of the twenty public computer terminals now on that floor. The library director argues that the change will increase the number of visitors the building serves each day, because demand for quiet study space in Riverton far exceeds the supply, while the periodicals room is seldom occupied by more than three people at once. The director's argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: The new study hall will be used mainly by students rather than by other Riverton residents.
No other building in Riverton could have been converted into study space at a lower cost.
The visitors gained by the study hall will outnumber those lost by removing the terminals.
The periodicals will be consulted more often once they have been moved to compact shelving.
Daily visitor count is the measure by which the library's director is formally evaluated.
explanation: The plan adds seating in one place and removes terminals in another, so a conclusion about the building's total daily visitors holds only if the gain is larger than the loss. Who uses the hall, what the conversion cost compared with alternatives, how often the periodicals are read afterward, and how the director is evaluated all leave that comparison untouched.

prompt: Halvorsen Freight measures its safety culture with an annual anonymous survey, and reports improvement because the share of employees describing management as responsive to safety concerns rose from 54 percent to 71 percent over three years. During the same three years the company cut the survey from sixty questions to twelve and began administering it during paid working hours instead of asking employees to complete it at home. The response rate rose from 38 percent to 84 percent. The safety director concludes that supervisors have in fact become markedly more responsive. The conclusion depends on the assumption that:
options: the employees who began responding once the survey moved into working hours do not differ systematically in their views from those who responded before
the twelve questions retained are the twelve that employees had found easiest to answer honestly
the results of the survey were reported to supervisors in each of the three years covered
no other freight company in the region achieved a comparable improvement over the same period
the number of recorded safety incidents at Halvorsen Freight also fell during the three years
explanation: The comparison is between two very different groups of respondents: a self-selected 38 percent who answered on their own time, and a much broader 84 percent who answered at work. A rise in the favorable share reflects changed supervision only if the newly reached employees hold views like those of the earlier respondents. Which questions were kept, whether supervisors saw the results, what competitors achieved, and the incident count are all beside that point.

prompt: The city of Bramwell reduced downtown congestion by charging drivers a fee to enter the central district on weekday mornings. Three years later, average travel times through that district had fallen by nineteen percent. The transportation committee of neighboring Keston has now proposed an identical fee, set at the same amount and applying during the same hours, and predicts a comparable reduction in Keston's downtown travel times. Keston's central district covers about the same area as Bramwell's and carries a similar volume of morning traffic. The committee's prediction assumes which of the following?
options: Bramwell set its fee at precisely the level that would produce the largest possible reduction in travel times.
Drivers in Keston are aware that a fee of this kind has already been operating in Bramwell for three years.
Travel time is the only measure of congestion that matters to the residents and businesses of Keston.
Keston's downtown businesses will not organize opposition to the fee before it can take effect.
Keston drivers have alternatives to driving downtown comparable to those Bramwell drivers had.
explanation: The prediction transfers a result from one city to another, so it holds only if the cities match in whatever made the fee work. A fee changes behavior by making some other option attractive, so Keston drivers must have options like the ones Bramwell drivers had. Whether Bramwell's fee was optimal, whether Keston drivers know about it, whether travel time is the only measure that matters, and whether businesses object are all irrelevant to that transfer.

prompt: A regional grid operator states that it can close its last coal plant in 2031 without risking winter shortfalls, provided that the offshore wind project now under construction delivers its full rated output and that the proposed transmission line to the neighboring grid is finished by 2030. Both projects have received every permit they require. The operator's planning report therefore concludes that the coal plant will be closed on schedule in 2031, and it recommends that the region procure no further generating capacity in the meantime. The recommendation depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: The offshore wind project will generate more electricity over a year than the coal plant it replaces generates.
The wind project and the transmission line will both be finished and operating on schedule.
The neighboring grid will have surplus power available for export during every winter after 2030.
A winter shortfall would do more damage to the region than a shortfall in any other season would.
No other coal plant anywhere in the region is scheduled to be closed before the end of 2031.
explanation: The operator's claim is conditional, and the report converts it into a flat prediction plus a recommendation to buy nothing else. The only thing offered in support of the two conditions being met is that permits have been granted, so the report assumes both of these two projects will in fact arrive on schedule. Annual output, the neighbor's surplus, the relative severity of winter, and other plants' schedules are not needed to get from the conditional claim to the recommendation.

prompt: Coastal Provisions, a grocery chain, will replace the plastic bags at its checkouts with paper bags in order to reduce the weight of the packaging waste its customers send to landfill. Company analysts note that customers currently carry home about four million plastic bags a year, and that the chain's contribution to landfill would fall if that plastic were eliminated. The paper bags will be given out at no charge, exactly as the plastic ones were. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument for the change?
options: Some customers of Coastal Provisions already bring reusable cloth bags with them when they shop.
Paper bags cost Coastal Provisions somewhat more per bag to purchase than plastic bags do, and the chain has decided to absorb the difference rather than raise its shelf prices.
A competing grocery chain in the same region removed plastic bags from its checkouts two years ago and reported no loss of customers as a result.
A paper bag strong enough to carry the same load weighs about six times what a plastic bag weighs, and shoppers use about the same number of either kind.
Plastic bags are occasionally reused by customers as liners for household waste bins.
explanation: The goal is stated in terms of weight, so a substitute that weighs six times as much per bag, used in the same numbers, makes the waste stream heavier rather than lighter and defeats the purpose of the change. Cloth bags, purchase cost, a competitor's decision and occasional reuse leave the weight comparison alone.

prompt: Between 2016 and 2023 the share of workplace injuries at Pellier Manufacturing occurring in the finishing department rose from 12 percent to 31 percent, while the share occurring in the foundry fell from 44 percent to 21 percent. The plant's safety officer concludes that the safety measures introduced in the foundry in 2017 have worked and that finishing has become the more dangerous department. She recommends transferring the foundry's remaining safety budget to finishing. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens her reasoning?
options: The foundry's workforce was cut by two thirds in 2018, while the finishing department's workforce did not change.
The finishing department installed new automated cutting equipment during the course of 2019, and the firm that supplies that equipment supplies most of the plants in the region.
Injuries occurring in the finishing department are on average less severe than foundry injuries, and fewer of them require a worker to miss a shift.
The current safety officer joined Pellier Manufacturing in 2017, the year the foundry measures began.
A number of injuries at the plant each year occur in departments other than the foundry and finishing.
explanation: Both figures are shares of a total, so either can move without any change in how dangerous a department is. If the foundry lost two thirds of its workers, its injury count would fall and its share with it, pushing finishing's share up even if finishing was exactly as safe as before. New equipment, injury severity, the officer's start date and injuries elsewhere do not explain the shift in shares.

prompt: A management consultancy studied the fifty independent manufacturers in the region that have stayed in business for more than forty years. Forty-one of the fifty fill the post of plant manager by promoting from within rather than by recruiting from outside, a far higher share than in the region's manufacturing sector as a whole. The consultancy's report concludes that promotion from within is what allows a manufacturer to survive over the long term, and it advises its own clients to stop recruiting plant managers externally. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the consultancy's conclusion?
options: The manufacturers that closed over those forty years promoted from within at a similar rate.
A plant manager recruited from outside needs several months to learn a plant's equipment.
The fifty manufacturers studied differ considerably in size and in what they produce.
At least one third of the fifty manufacturers have changed owners in the past forty years.
Promoting from within costs a manufacturer less in recruitment fees than hiring outside does.
explanation: The study looked only at the firms that lasted, so a practice common among them is evidence of nothing until the firms that failed are counted too. If those closed firms promoted from within just as often, the practice fails to separate the survivors from anyone and the advice rests on the way the sample was chosen. A shorter learning period and lower recruitment fees are reasons to promote internally and so run with the conclusion rather than against it. Variety of size and product, and a change of owner, leave the missing comparison missing.

prompt: A management consultancy studied 200 companies that had adopted a decentralized decision-making structure, and found that those still using the structure ten years later reported revenue growth well above the average for their industries. The consultancy concludes that decentralization reliably produces superior growth, and recommends the structure to its clients without qualification. Its report notes that the companies studied were drawn from nine industries in four countries, so the finding is unlikely to be an artifact of conditions in any single market. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: Some of the nine industries in the study grew considerably faster overall than others did during the decade.
The consultancy earns substantial fees from advising its clients on organizational restructuring projects.
The decentralized firms in the sample were on average younger than the industry peers they were compared with.
Revenue growth is an imperfect proxy for profitability in several of the nine industries studied.
Only 70 of the 200 companies were still using the structure after ten years, and most of the rest abandoned it after long stretches of weak results.
explanation: The finding is drawn only from the companies that kept the structure, so the poor performers have been filtered out of the measurement before it is taken. If most of the 200 dropped the structure after years of weak results, the surviving group is defined partly by success, and its growth says little about what decentralization does on average. Uneven industry growth, the consultancy's fees, firm age and the choice of metric all leave that filtering in place.

prompt: The town of Marbury will eliminate the fare on its three bus routes, funding the service from parking revenue instead, in order to reduce the number of cars entering the town center on weekday mornings. Transit planners predict that ridership will roughly double and that morning car traffic will fall noticeably as a result. Surveys of Marbury residents who say they rarely take the bus indicate that the fare, though modest, is mentioned more often than any other reason for not riding. Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the planners' prediction?
options: Marbury's parking revenue is projected to cover the full cost of operating the three routes for at least the next five years.
In two comparable towns that eliminated bus fares, most of the riders gained had previously driven into the town center.
Marbury's buses run at roughly half of their seating capacity in the morning, so the three routes could absorb a large increase in riders without new vehicles.
The town council approved the change by a wide margin after holding two public hearings on it.
The routes served by Marbury's three bus lines were last redesigned more than fifteen years ago.
explanation: The prediction has two steps, and the weak one is the second: more riders reduce car traffic only if the new riders come out of cars rather than off the sidewalk or a bicycle. Evidence from comparable towns that the gained riders were previously drivers supplies exactly that link. Funding, spare capacity, the council vote and the age of the route map say nothing about where the new riders come from.

prompt: Agronomists at a research station propose that a fungal treatment applied to wheat seed protects seedlings from a root rot that costs growers in the district about a tenth of their yield each year. In field trials, treated plots lost 4 percent of their yield to root rot while untreated plots lost 11 percent. Skeptics point out that the treated and untreated plots were not adjacent to one another, and that soil moisture, which strongly affects the severity of root rot, varies considerably across the station's land. Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the agronomists' proposal?
options: The fungal treatment costs a grower far less per hectare than the value of the yield it is said to protect, even in a mild year.
Root rot has been recorded in the wheat-growing districts of the region for more than sixty years.
Commercially available wheat varieties differ from one another in their natural susceptibility to root rot.
The station's agronomists have published earlier work on seed treatments for other cereal diseases.
Soil moisture readings taken through the season were nearly identical across all of the plots.
explanation: The objection is that a factor other than the treatment could differ between the two sets of plots, and the answer removes it: equal moisture across the plots rules out the specific rival the skeptics named, which leaves the treatment as the difference between the two sets. Cost, the history of the disease, varietal differences and the researchers' publication record leave the objection standing.

prompt: Excavators at a Bronze Age coastal site found a workshop containing crucibles, unworked tin ingots and stone molds for casting bronze axes. Tin occurs nowhere in the surrounding region. The site director argues that the settlement was a manufacturing center that imported raw tin over long distances and then exported finished bronze goods, rather than a market that received metal and passed it onward in the form in which it arrived. Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the site director's argument?
options: Axes matching the shape of the workshop's molds have been recovered from a dozen distant sites, none of which has produced a mold of that form.
The unworked tin ingots bear incised marks closely resembling marks on ingots recovered from a contemporary shipwreck in the same sea.
The settlement's harbor was deep enough to accommodate the largest sailing vessels in use during the period.
Bronze was worth more per unit of weight than either of the two metals from which it was made.
Several of the crucibles from the workshop show traces of copper in addition to traces of tin.
explanation: The claim to be supported is about export of finished goods, not merely about local casting, so the useful evidence is finished axes of this workshop's distinctive form turning up far away in places that could not have made them. Marks on the ingots and traces in the crucibles bear on import and on casting, which nobody disputes, and harbor depth and the relative value of bronze are consistent with a settlement that only traded metal onward.

prompt: The Ferndale plant employs technicians, engineers and administrative staff. Every technician at the plant is certified to service turbines, and some of the technicians are also certified to service generators. Generator certification requires a separate examination, which the plant administers twice a year and which any employee may sit. All employees at Ferndale who hold generator certification, whatever their job title, are paid a premium above the base technician wage, and that premium has been part of the plant's pay structure since it opened. If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Every technician employed at the Ferndale plant is paid a premium above the base technician wage.
Only employees whose job title is technician hold generator certification at the Ferndale plant.
Some technicians at the Ferndale plant are paid a premium above the base technician wage.
Technicians certified to service generators are not also certified to service turbines.
Most of the employees at the Ferndale plant are certified to service turbines.
explanation: Some technicians hold generator certification, and everyone with that certification receives the premium, so some technicians receive the premium. Nothing establishes that all technicians do, that only technicians hold the certification, or how technicians compare in number with engineers and administrative staff, and every technician is certified for turbines whatever else they hold.

prompt: A regional airline reported the following about its flights last year. Sixty percent of them departed from its main hub. Eighty percent of them arrived within fifteen minutes of the scheduled arrival time. Every flight that arrived more than fifteen minutes late had departed late. Fewer than half of the flights that departed late were flights out of the main hub. The airline operated no flights other than those covered by these figures. If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Most of the flights that departed late were flights out of the airline's main hub.
Every flight that departed late arrived more than fifteen minutes behind its scheduled time.
More of the airline's flights arrived late than departed late over the course of the year.
At least 20 percent of the airline's flights departed late.
Fewer than 20 percent of the flights out of the main hub departed late last year.
explanation: Twenty percent of flights arrived more than fifteen minutes late, and every one of those had departed late, so late departures account for at least that same 20 percent. The claim that most late departures were hub flights contradicts the figures given. A late departure need not produce a late arrival, late arrivals are a subset of late departures rather than a larger group, and the figures fix no rate of late departure for hub flights specifically.

prompt: A national household survey found that 45 percent of households own at least one bicycle and that 30 percent own at least one motorcycle. Among the households that own at least one bicycle, exactly 20 percent also own at least one motorcycle. The survey reached a representative sample of households in every region of the country, and every household in the sample answered both questions. If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: More than half of the country's households own neither a bicycle nor a motorcycle.
Fewer than one third of the households that own a motorcycle also own a bicycle.
A household that owns a motorcycle is more likely to own a bicycle than a household chosen at random is.
Exactly 75 percent of households own a bicycle, a motorcycle, or both of them.
Twenty percent of all households in the country own both a bicycle and a motorcycle.
explanation: Households owning both come to 20 percent of the 45 percent that own a bicycle, which is 9 percent of all households. Those 9 points sit inside the 30 percent that own a motorcycle, so the share of motorcycle owners who also own a bicycle is 9 out of 30, which is below one third. Households owning neither come to 34 percent, ownership of one or the other or both comes to 66 percent, motorcycle owners are less likely than average to own a bicycle, and the 20 percent figure is a share of bicycle owners rather than of all households.

prompt: A newspaper column argues as follows. The telephone company advertises its new plan as free of charge for the first three months, but the plan is not free at all. A customer must sign a contract lasting two years, and the total the customer pays over those two years is greater than what the company charged for the plan it offered last year. Anything that costs a customer money is not free. The company's advertisement is therefore dishonest. Which of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the column's reasoning?
options: It relies on figures about the previous year's prices that it makes no attempt to verify.
It assumes that every customer reads the terms of a contract before agreeing to sign it.
It draws a conclusion about every plan the company advertises from evidence that concerns only the terms of the one plan introduced this year.
It treats the opinion of one newspaper columnist as though it were an established fact.
It treats a claim about the cost of an introductory period as a claim about the cost of the whole contract.
explanation: The advertisement says the first three months are free, and the column refutes something else: that the two-year contract as a whole is free. Once the two claims are kept apart, the total paid over two years is entirely consistent with the advertised offer, so no dishonesty has been shown. Unverified figures, contract reading, generalization and the columnist's standing are not what goes wrong here.

prompt: A district health board rejected a proposal to add fluoride to the public water supply, stating the following. No study submitted to this board has demonstrated that fluoridation at the proposed concentration is free of long-term harm. Until such a demonstration is produced, we must conclude that fluoridation at that concentration is unsafe. Since our duty is to the residents we serve, we are obliged to reject the proposal. The board's reasoning is most vulnerable to which of the following criticisms?
options: It treats the absence of a demonstration that something is safe as a demonstration that it is unsafe.
It assumes without argument that residents of the district would oppose fluoridation if they were consulted.
It generalizes from studies of a single concentration to conclusions about every possible concentration.
It confuses a claim about what the board is obliged to do with a claim about what the evidence shows.
It relies on the testimony of experts whose independence from the water industry it has not established.
explanation: The premise reports only that no submitted study has established safety, and the board converts that gap in its own file into a positive finding of danger. A question that has not been settled either way cannot support a conclusion in one direction. Nothing is said about residents' opinions or about any expert testimony, and the generalization runs from many concentrations to one rather than the reverse.

prompt: Bellhaven Transit is deciding whether to replace its diesel buses with electric ones. An electric bus costs about 40 percent more to purchase than a diesel bus of the same capacity, but costs roughly 60 percent less per kilometer to fuel and maintain, and the two types have similar service lives. The agency's finance office concludes that replacing each diesel bus with an electric one as it reaches the end of its service life will reduce the agency's total costs over the next twenty years. Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating that conclusion?
options: Whether electric buses produce noticeably less noise than diesel buses do on residential streets
How many kilometers a typical Bellhaven bus travels over the course of its service life
Whether the manufacturer of Bellhaven's current diesel buses also produces electric models
How many passengers Bellhaven's buses carry during the weekday morning peak period
Whether other transit agencies of a similar size have already adopted electric buses
explanation: The argument trades a larger purchase price against a smaller cost per kilometer, so which side wins depends entirely on how many kilometers the bus runs before it is retired. Few enough and the purchase premium is never recovered. Noise, the identity of the manufacturer, peak ridership and what peer agencies have done leave that tradeoff undecided.

prompt: For six years the Halloway Trust has funded a program that places recent graduates in rural teaching posts. The trust reports that 68 percent of the teachers it placed were still teaching in a rural district three years after placement, against a published national three-year retention rate of 51 percent for rural teaching posts. On that basis the trust concludes that its program raises retention, and it is asking donors to fund an expansion into two additional states. Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the trust's conclusion?
options: How many graduates applied to the Halloway Trust program in each of the six years it has operated
Whether the teachers placed by the trust are paid more than other teachers in the same rural districts, and whether any such difference is met by the trust rather than by the district itself
What proportion of the teachers placed by the trust are still teaching ten years after placement
Whether the national retention figure, like the trust's own figure, counts a teacher who moves to a rural district in another state as having stayed
Whether the two additional states the trust proposes to enter currently face a shortage of rural teachers
explanation: The whole argument is a comparison of two percentages, and it collapses if the two are not counting the same thing. A figure that credits any continued rural teaching will sit above one that credits only staying in the original district, and the gap between 68 and 51 could be an artifact of that difference alone. Application volume, pay, ten-year retention and shortages in the target states do not tell us whether the two numbers are comparable.

prompt:
Passage: "When central banks began announcing numerical inflation targets in the late twentieth century, the innovation looked modest. A bank would state a rate it intended to achieve, publish forecasts, and explain its decisions. Nothing in the arrangement gave the bank new instruments, since interest rates remained the principal lever. Advocates argued that the value lay elsewhere, in expectations. If firms and workers believed that inflation would settle near the announced figure, they would write that figure into wage agreements and price lists, and the belief would help produce the outcome. On this account a target is less a promise about policy than a coordinating device for private decisions.

Critics accepted the mechanism but questioned its scope. A target anchors expectations only while the public believes the bank will act on it, and belief of that kind is built slowly and spent quickly. Several banks that adopted targets during calm decades were praised for a stability that owed at least as much to falling commodity prices and expanding trade as to any announcement. When those conditions reversed, the same institutions found that announcements alone moved very little.

A further objection concerns what the target leaves out. A single figure for consumer prices says nothing about asset prices, credit growth, or the distribution of income, and a bank judged only on that figure has little reason to attend to them. Defenders reply that assigning one instrument to one objective is what makes the arrangement accountable, and that a mandate broadened to cover everything would in practice constrain nothing. The dispute is less about whether targets work than about what work they were ever meant to do." The passage suggests that the effectiveness of an inflation target depends primarily on which of the following?
options: Whether the public believes the bank will act to meet the announced figure
Whether the central bank possesses policy instruments other than the interest rate
Whether commodity prices fall during the years in which the target is in force
Whether the announced figure is low enough to keep wage agreements from rising

Ambro's operations director concludes that a majority of the company's passengers consider the service unpunctual, and he has made punctuality the first priority for the coming year.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the operations director's conclusion?
options: Ambro carried slightly fewer passengers last year than it carried in the year before.
Some passengers filled in and returned more than one comment card during the year.
A passenger who is dissatisfied with a service is far more likely to return a comment card than a satisfied passenger is.
Ambro's trains arrived within five minutes of their scheduled time on most days last year, and the delays that did occur fell almost entirely on one line and one time of day.
Rail companies operating in the neighboring regions do not distribute comment cards, so Ambro has no outside figure against which to set its own result.
explanation: The director treats the returned cards as though they represented passengers generally. If dissatisfied passengers return cards at a much higher rate, the returned cards overstate dissatisfaction and cannot support a claim about the majority of passengers. Whether the trains actually ran on time does not bear on what passengers think, and the remaining statements affect neither the sample nor the conclusion drawn from it.

prompt: Sales of electric delivery vans in the province have doubled in each of the last four years, and electric vans now make up eight percent of the delivery fleet on the road. The provincial haulage association projects that on the same trajectory they will make up more than half the fleet within four more years. On the strength of that projection it has asked the province to begin converting the roadside inspection stations to handle electric drivetrains, and to pay for the work by cutting the budget for diesel emissions testing. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the association's projection?
options: The province's roadside inspection stations were last refitted more than twenty years ago, before the first electric van reached the road.
An electric van still costs more to buy than a diesel van of comparable capacity, and that gap has not narrowed in four years.
The vans sold so far serve short depot routes, and almost every such route already has one.
Several manufacturers have announced longer-range electric vans for delivery in two years.
The number of diesel vans registered in the province has fallen for three years running.
explanation: A projection that extends a trend has to assume the conditions that produced it will hold. If the doubling came from converting one narrow part of the fleet, and that part is now almost fully converted, the next doubling would have to come from routes the vehicles do not yet suit, so the trajectory breaks well short of half the fleet. Longer-range models and a shrinking diesel count both push the other way. Price is a standing condition through the four years of doubling rather than a change, and the age of the stations bears on the cost of the work, not on the forecast.

The finance office of Merrick Hospital reports that each of the hospital's six departments has idle equipment time and that each could therefore cut its own spending by at least eight percent by scheduling procedures more tightly. The office concludes that the hospital as a whole could cut its spending by at least eight percent if all six departments were required to schedule their procedures more tightly.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the finance office's conclusion?
options: A department can schedule tightly only by using shared operating rooms in hours that another department would then have to give up.
Two of the six departments have already begun to schedule their procedures more tightly.
The hospital's spending on staff has risen faster in recent years than its spending on equipment, and staff costs are now the larger of the two.
An hour of idle equipment time costs considerably more in some of the six departments than in others, and the two largest departments are the most expensive.
Patients at the hospital sometimes cancel scheduled procedures at short notice.
explanation: What each department can achieve on its own does not carry over to all of them at once if the savings draw on a resource they share. If tighter scheduling requires operating room hours that the departments must take from one another, the six savings cannot be added, and the hospital wide figure does not follow. Partial adoption, differing costs of idle time, and occasional cancellations leave the reasoning intact.

A national agency reports that the share of workers in insecure employment fell from nineteen percent to fourteen percent over five years, and the labor minister cites the figure as evidence that her reforms have made work more secure. The agency classifies a worker as insecurely employed if the worker holds a contract that is due to expire within twelve months. The agency has surveyed the same population by the same method throughout the five years.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the minister's use of the figure?
options: The agency's survey now covers a smaller sample of workers than it covered five years ago.
Wages in the sectors with the most insecure employment rose slowly over the five year period.
The reforms also changed the way that income from self employment is taxed.
Employers increasingly replaced twelve month contracts with rolling contracts that either party may end at two weeks notice.
Workers under thirty are more likely than older workers to hold a contract due to expire within twelve months.
explanation: The minister treats the agency's category as though it measured security. If employers moved workers onto rolling contracts that can be ended at two weeks notice, those workers leave the measured category while becoming less secure, so the falling figure is consistent with no improvement at all. The sample size claim is ruled out by the stated consistency of method, and wages, taxation, and the age profile of insecure work do not bear on what the figure captures.

Brine loses nearly all of its effect if it is applied after snow has started to fall. The council's three trucks can treat the entire road network in six hours, and brine costs less per treated kilometer than salt does. The council concludes that the switch will halve salt use without leaving the roads less safe than they are now.

The council's conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Brine will remain cheaper per treated kilometer than road salt for several more winters, and the saving will be large enough to cover the cost of storing and mixing the solution.
The council will usually know that snow is coming early enough to treat the network before it begins.
The council's three trucks are newer than the trucks used by neighboring towns.
Residents of Dunmore have asked the council more than once to reduce the salt it spreads, citing damage to roadside trees and to parked vehicles.
Snowfalls in Dunmore usually begin during daylight hours rather than overnight.
explanation: The plan works only if the brine is on the road before the snow, and the trucks need six hours to cover the network. So the council must be able to see a snowfall coming with at least that much warning. Relative cost is already stated and is not what the safety claim rests on, and the remaining choices concern equipment age, public opinion, and the hour of day, none of which is required.

Rell Publishing spends more each year on warehousing its printed backlist than it earns from selling those titles. The finance director proposes to destroy the remaining stock of every backlist title that sold fewer than fifty copies last year, a step that would cut the company's warehousing costs by a third. She concludes that making this change would improve the company's annual result.

The finance director's conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: No backlist title that sold fewer than fifty copies last year would sell more than fifty copies next year.
Destroying the remaining stock would cost the company nothing at all.
The backlist titles that sell well are stored in the same warehouse as the slow selling ones, and the warehouse is charged for by the square meter.
Rell Publishing's competitors also keep large printed backlists in warehouses.
The revenue given up on the destroyed titles will be smaller than the warehousing cost the change saves.
explanation: The proposal saves a warehousing cost and gives up whatever those titles would have earned, so it improves the result only if the saving is the larger of the two. The first choice is stronger than the argument needs, since a few better selling titles are compatible with a net gain, and disposal being entirely free is likewise more than is required. Where the stock sits and what competitors do are beside the point.

On the same routes Vendal competes with two carriers that continue to include a meal in the fare. Vendal's management concludes that the change will raise the profit the airline earns on those routes.

Vendal's conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Passengers flying two hour routes eat less than passengers flying longer routes.
Neither of the two competing carriers will withdraw its own complimentary meal.
Vendal will not lose so many passengers to the competing carriers that the loss outweighs the saving.
Vendal's costs on routes longer than two hours will remain unchanged next year.
Vendal's paid menu will be priced above what the food on it costs the airline to supply.
explanation: The saving is real, but two rivals still include a meal, so passengers who care about it can move. Profit rises only if the revenue lost with those passengers is smaller than eleven dollars for each passenger retained. What competitors do next is not required by the argument, and a profitable menu and the costs of other routes would each be welcome without being necessary.

A study of one hundred technology firms found that firms whose engineers spend more than a quarter of their working time on projects of their own choosing filed more patents per engineer than the remaining firms did. The chief executive of Halden Systems, whose engineers file few patents and currently spend no working time on projects of their own choosing, will therefore require every Halden engineer to spend two full days each week on a project of that engineer's own choosing, in order to raise the firm's patent output per engineer.

The chief executive's plan depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Time that engineers must set aside for work of their own choosing yields patents as readily as time they set aside voluntarily.
Halden Systems employs fewer engineers than the average firm covered by the study, and it files fewer patents in total than any of them.
Patents filed per engineer is the best available measure of a technology firm's innovation.
The firms covered by the study did not differ from one another in the laboratory resources that they made available to their engineers.
Halden's engineers currently spend less than a quarter of their working time on projects they choose.
explanation: The study describes firms where engineers spend such time, while the plan compels them to. The conclusion holds only if compelled self directed time behaves like the time the study observed. The size of the firm and the merits of patent counting are not needed, uniform resources across a hundred firms is far stronger than the argument requires, and the stimulus states Halden's current allocation outright, so it is not a hidden assumption.

No newspaper other than these two was published in Kelso during those years.

options: The Courier's presses were requisitioned again at some point after 1918.
The Herald was the more widely read of the two Kelso newspapers.
No issue of the Courier printed before 1912 survives anywhere outside the archive.
The archive acquired the issues of both newspapers in the year each issue was printed.
For some months, the archive holds issues of the Herald and of no other Kelso newspaper.

So for those months the only Kelso issues in the archive are the Herald's. Readership, later requisitions, survival elsewhere, and the timing of acquisition are all matters the statements do not settle.

Two thirds of last year's grants went to organizations that had received a Tarn grant at some earlier time. Every organization that had received a Tarn grant at an earlier time is based in Ledd province. The foundation awarded no organization more than one grant last year.

options: Every organization based in Ledd province has at some time received a Tarn grant.
Exactly one third of last year's grants went to organizations based outside Ledd province.
At least two thirds of last year's grants went to organizations based in Ledd province.
The foundation awarded more grants last year than it awarded in any earlier year.
No organization based outside Ledd province applied for a Tarn grant last year.

The region has issued no new permit since 2015, and no permit may be transferred from one farm to another. Three quarters of the region's farms are smaller than forty hectares. The total volume of aquifer water drawn by farms in the region has risen in every year since 2015, and rainfall has been stable throughout.

If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: Some farms smaller than forty hectares now draw water from the aquifer.
The total number of farms in the Rensa region has fallen since 2015.
Farms in the region have planted crops that require more water than the crops grown in 2015.
The average volume of aquifer water drawn per irrigating farm has risen since 2015.
Rainfall in the Rensa region will remain stable in the coming years.
explanation: Only permit holders draw from the aquifer, no permit has been issued since 2015, and none may be transferred, so the number of farms drawing water cannot have grown. A rising total divided by a number of farms that did not increase gives a rising average per farm. Small farms drawing water is ruled out by the permit rule, and nothing here fixes the number of farms in the region, the crops planted, or future rainfall.
